newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Key ex-USSR grain producers set for recovery.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Key ex-USSR grain producers set for recovery.

text.p: Early grain harvest forecasts for the former Soviet Union's top three producers point to rising production and stable regional trade patterns this year, industry officials said on Friday.

Although crops are still vulnerable to the vagaries of the weather, the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) will have no problem meeting its grain needs this year, based on the early outlook for Russia, Ukraine and Kazakhstan.
"At this early stage, growing conditions are good in all three of these countries," said Arkady Zlochevsky, chief executive of the Moscow-based private OGO commodities firm.

Russia has officially forecast a net grain crop of at least 70 million tonnes this year, little changed from the 69.3 million produced in 1996. Both figures are rather poor, but declining livestock numbers have pushed consumption down.
"We anticipate the Russian crop figure will be largely unchanged from last year's figure of around 69.5 million tonnes," said Daniel Day-Robinson of commodity consultants Day-Robinson Ltd.
Viktor Trenin of the State Meteorological Service said earlier in the week that with just four weeks to go before farmers mount their combines, weather conditions were ideal.

"Everything remains very favourable (for the crops)," he said, adding recent rains had helped farmers in the European part of Russia. But low moisture levels might still threaten some areas in Siberia.
"The crucial time for that is July," Trenin said.
Ukraine's harvest looks set to recover strongly from last year's disastrous output, according to western analysts.
Severe drought saw production slump last year to a paltry 25.4 million tonnes, but this year's crop could hit official targets of 35 million, they said.
Drought also plagued Kazakhstan's agricultural sector in 1996, but analysts are looking for a recovery to 14 million tonnes this year from 1996's 11.6 million.
But grain traders and analysts added the weather in Kazakhstan was especially unpredictable, since drought conditions can often give way to heavy rain or even snow during the autumn harvest.
"I still think it is too early to start predicting the size of the Kazakh crop," said Andrei Sizov of SovEcon Ltd, a private consultancy in Moscow.
Zlochevsky said Russia would still have to import several million tonnes of grain this year, up to 80 percent of which would come from within the CIS, mainly Kazakhstan.
"A major part of Russia's grain imports tend to come from Kazakhstan, and this will continue," he said. "It is less profitable to import from Ukraine."
While Kazakhstan may continue to dominate Russian grain imports, trade between the two countries in key products wheat and barley is seen falling due to rising Russian production.
One senior Moscow-based grain trader said Russian import needs could be way below the some analysts' forecasts for 1997.

"Kazakhstan may supply small amounts to neighbouring Russian regions, and there could be small imports of corn (maize) for the poultry industry, but this year there may by no significant grain imports to speak of at all," the trader said.
CIS grain minnows Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan are looking for higher production this year and to reduce dependence on former Soviet allies.

Uzbekistan aims to produce 4.0 million tonnes in 1997 from 3.54 million in 1996. Zair Latypov, deputy head of the Agriculture Ministry's grain department, said earlier this week the official 1997 target was "reasonable."
Turkmenistan has set a grain output target of 1.2 million tonnes in 1997, up sharply from just 480,000 tonnes last year.
Higher exports from CIS countries to other regions were therefore on the cards, trader said.
